case.case_title: Senaratne v. Punya de Silva and Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1995] 1 Sri L.R. 272

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s detention prior to being produced before a Magistrate was lawful and complied with the time limits and procedures required by Article 13(2) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that his detention on 23 December 1994 was illegal and violated his fundamental right to freedom from arbitrary detention under Articles 13(1) and/or 13(2) because he was not produced before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondent did not provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay in producing the petitioner before the Magistrate but contended the arrest and detention were lawful.
key_facts: Petitioner was arrested at about 9 a.m. on 23 December 1994.
He was produced before the Magistrate at about 2.45 p.m. the same day and released on bail.
The delay in production was not explained and was found unnecessary and unreasonable by the Court.
Sections 36 and 37 of the Code of Criminal Procedure require prompt production before a Magistrate within 24 hours excluding travel time.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: Article 13(2) requires that any person detained be brought before a judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law without unnecessary delay, and detention beyond a reasonable time violates this right regardless of the lawfulness of the arrest.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the petitioner’s detention for several hours before being produced was unnecessary and unreasonable, thus violating Article 13(2). The production at 2.45 p.m. did not comply with the statutory provisions and constitutional mandate.
principles_established: Detention beyond a reasonable time without judicial intervention violates Article 13(2).
The 24-hour limit for production before a Magistrate is strict and excludes travel time.
Lawfulness of arrest is irrelevant to the requirement of prompt production.
Strict interpretation of 'reasonable time' is required to safeguard personal liberty.
precedents_cited: Mahinda Rajapakse and Vasudeva Nanayakkara v. Chief Inspector Karunaratne & Others

outcome.holding: The Court held that the delay in producing the petitioner before the Magistrate was unnecessary and unreasonable, violating Article 13(2) of the Constitution.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Declaration of violation of Article 13(2) fundamental right and order for costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) is central to the Court’s finding that the petitioner’s detention was unlawful due to delay in judicial production, which is a key aspect of the fundamental right to personal liberty.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was detained from about 9 a.m. until 2.45 p.m. before being produced to the Magistrate, an unnecessary and unreasonable delay violating the statutory and constitutional requirements under Article 13(2).
